title: HTTP client stack
issueTitle: HTTP client stack for BotTools: suspend transport, outbound-URL guard, response cache, call budget and test fakes
function: BotTools needs a suspend HTTP stack: a transport, an outbound-URL guard, a response cache, a call budget and test fakes. This tracking issue designs it as a new Kotlin Multiplatform module `webtools-http`, a feeds module `webtools-feeds` on top of it, the shared `build-logic` with the Java 11 floor that folds in #47, and their documentation, and builds it as eleven units, each a sub-issue planned and built on its own board.

wip.detail: Units 1 to 3 have landed: #61 (`build-logic`) through PR #74 as 1e27071, #47 (`java-floor`) through PR #76 as 3949b52, and #62 (`http-core`) through PR #82 as 7de8207, which adds `webtools-http` 1.0.0, new and unreleased. Unit 4, #63 (`test-support`), is in progress: its run started on 2026-10-25 at the plan step, a re-pass against architecture.md §6.7, §6.1 and §11 and impact.md §7. Unit 5, #64 (`url-policy`), is up next. Units 6 to 11 follow in landing order.

gap.summary: No HTTP stack exists. `Connector` is the only HTTP client: a blocking, stateful line reader over `URLConnection` that sets the JVM-wide `http.agent` on every connect and calls `Unirest.setTimeouts(0, 0)` in its `init`. Nothing offers a suspend request, a typed failure model or a transport port.

options.name: Open failure hierarchy in `kotlin.Result`, builders over `internal` constructors, one opt-in marker through `@SubclassOptInRequired`
options.why: Adding a failure leaf or a builder property never breaks a consumer's compiled code, and the supplied defaults are usable without opting in.

options.name: A sealed failure root, or enums for library-produced reasons
options.why: Each added leaf or entry is a compile error in a consumer's exhaustive `when` and a runtime `NoWhenBranchMatchedException` in a compiled one.

options.name: Flat constructors with defaulted parameters plus hidden deprecated overloads
options.why: A permanent overload per addition kept correct by hand; `@IntroducedAt` is Kotlin 2.3+.

options.name: `kotlin.time.Clock`/`Instant` or kotlinx-datetime in signatures
options.why: An error-level opt-in on every 2.2.x consumer, and the budget needs no calendar arithmetic.

options.name: `fun interface` for `WallClock`
options.why: A `fun interface` cannot carry the subclass gate; one rule for every seam.

options.name: An opaque `Scheduling` type in place of `CoroutineDispatcher`, keeping coroutines `implementation`
options.why: A consumer could no longer pass its own dispatcher, and the coroutines runtime is part of what a suspend API is.

options.name: kotlin-logging in `commonMain`
options.why: A startup line and a runtime dependency on every consumer, with no gain on one published target; an `internal expect fun` seam is the smallest thing that logs.

options.name: A published `js` target instead of check-only modules
options.why: A coordinate and a klib nothing consumes, Node and Yarn downloads for tests, and a published surface the requirements do not name.
options.wins: The day a non-JVM consumer exists.

options.name: KGP's built-in `abiValidation` instead of BCV
options.why: Experimental on 2.2.0 and its DSL changed by 2.4.

verdict.defense: One system: one new module's additive API. Its plan starts with the compile proof of the marker, a gated interface, a default naming it and a consumer without opt-in.
tests: Level 4a in `commonTest`: parsing, validation, query encoding
`jvmTest`: the `Url`-vs-`HttpUrl` differential
risks: The public surface has not been compiled; the opt-in behaviour comes from compiler test data and one JVM-only measurement

asBuilt.summary: Landed through PR #82 as 7de8207 (#62): `webtools-http` is the first module on the multiplatform convention, with `explicitApi()`, its ABI dump and `kotlinx-coroutines-core` as its one `api` dependency. It holds the opt-in marker, the failure model with both reason vocabularies, the request and response types with `Url`, and the gated ports `HttpTransport` and `WallClock` with `WallClock.System`. `webtools-http-commoncheck` compiles its `commonMain` for `js()` with no environment through the new `webtools.kotlin-common-check` plugin, so `build` downloads no Node.js and the root project gains no task. `webtools-http` 1.0.0 is new and unreleased; no version moved.

changes.what: The check plugin `webtools.kotlin-common-check` calls `js()` with no environment, in place of the `js { nodejs { testTask { enabled = false } } }` of architecture §3, §6.1 and §6.8, so the root project gains no task and unit 4's open point on where the publication check attaches stands.

gap.summary: Nothing decides which URLs may be fetched. OkHttp never consults `Dns` for a digits-and-dots or colon host, so a resolver guard alone misses every IP-literal host, and native redirect follow-up reached `169.254.169.254` through a resolver guard.
evidence: research/http-transport.md — interceptors run after the connect

options.name: A closed `Trusted`/`Untrusted` pair checked in three layers: pre-check, resolver guard, socket factory
options.why: Every layer alone leaks (measured on 39 host forms); together the socket factory backstops the resolver guard.

options.name: A resolver guard only, or a network interceptor or `EventListener` as the guard
options.why: A resolver guard misses every IP-literal host; interceptors run after the connect and a listener cannot veto.

options.name: A consumer-implemented `UrlGuard` seam at 1.0.0
options.why: A callback that can return "allow" can silently defeat `Untrusted`, and no real consumer has shaped the seam.

tests: Level 4a in `commonTest`: every IANA row's first and last address, the host-form catalogue, the published bypass vectors
`jvmTest`: the JDK-predicate-gap and differential tests

gap.summary: OkHttp 5.5.0 re-sends a `503` carrying `Retry-After: 0` and a `421` regardless of client flags, strips only `Authorization` on a cross-host redirect, and a body read after `executeAsync` returns is not cancellable (29.4 s against 0 ms).

options.name: A manual redirect loop, a fail-closed one-exchange guard and a capped body read inside the callback

`./gradlew build` adds `verifyJavaFloor` on every published module, `apiCheck` on the new modules and the check-only JS compiles, which compile only: their `js` target has no environment, so no test task and no Node.js.
